title: Smash Burger
subtitle: Double smashed beef patties with crispy lacy edges
excerpt: A smash burger is made by placing a ball of beef mince on a very hot flat surface and immediately pressing (smashing) it flat with a spatula. The thin patty develops a deeply caramelised crust with crispy lacy edges in about 90 seconds per side. Two thin patties stacked with melted cheese is the classic build.
sourceNotes: The smash burger technique was popularised by the American Smashburger chain (founded 2007) but the method of pressing thin patties on a griddle dates to diner cooking of the mid-20th century. The technique maximises the Maillard reaction by creating maximum contact between the meat and the hot surface.

recipe.temperatureNote: cast-iron or flat griddle pan, screaming hot

content.text: The smash burger is a technique. The ball of beef goes straight onto the hottest possible flat surface and is pressed flat within 10 seconds. The thin patty makes maximum contact with the heat, producing a broad dark crust and crispy lacy edges where the fat renders out and crisps. Do not press a second time once smashed: the crust forms in those first seconds and pressing again disrupts it. Two thin patties is better than one thick one.

items.prepNote: 20% fat, formed into 4 balls of 80 g each
raw, very finely sliced into rings

content.text: Heat a cast-iron pan or flat griddle over maximum heat for at least 5 minutes. It must be smoking hot.

Season each ball of beef with salt and pepper on all sides. Place 2 balls in the pan (do not crowd). Using a flat spatula, smash each ball down as hard as possible until the patty is about 1 cm thick. Do this within 10 seconds of the ball hitting the pan.
Cook undisturbed for 60 to 90 seconds until a dark brown crust has formed and the edges look dry and crispy. Scrape up and flip. The patty may stick slightly: scrape under it firmly.
Place a slice of cheese on each patty immediately after flipping. Cook for 45 seconds more. Stack 2 patties together (cheese melts between them). Repeat with remaining beef balls.
Toast the buns in the pan for 30 seconds cut-side down. Build: pickles and onion on the base, stacked patties, ketchup and mustard on the lid. Eat immediately.

items.symptom: Patty sticks to the pan and tears apart when flipped
items.cause: The crust had not fully formed before flipping, or the pan was not hot enough
items.fix: Wait until the patty releases easily before flipping. A properly developed crust will release from the pan. A stuck patty needs more time.

items.cause: Pan not hot enough or patty not pressed thin enough
items.fix: The pan must be screaming hot before anything goes in. Press the patty as flat as possible when smashing: the lacy edges come from the thin parts of the patty.

content.text: A smash burger maximises the Maillard reaction, the browning that occurs when proteins and sugars are exposed to high heat. A thin patty has a higher surface-area-to-volume ratio than a thick one, meaning more of the meat is in contact with the hot surface and more of it browns. This is why smash burgers taste beefier than thicker patties: more crust, more flavour.
